state.title: Atlas-SDK
state.vision: Atlas-SDK is a general-purpose application runtime and plugin platform. It owns the orchestration lifecycle — discovery, validation, registration, dependency and contract resolution, initialization, running, shutdown — and is the source of truth for it, so a host does not implement a competing lifecycle, registry or contract system. Plugins are self-contained capability providers that declare stable identity, version, capabilities, contracts provided, contracts required and lifecycle behaviour; the same plugin must run under different Atlas hosts unchanged. Plugins never import or reach into each other. They communicate only through SDK-managed Contracts (stable identity and version, request/response, command/result, query/structured result) and Events (facts that occurred, versioned, many subscribers, no dependency between them). Capabilities are explicit and machine-readable, sufficient to answer what a plugin provides, what a host supports, what activation requires and what permission a capability needs. Plugins receive platform services — authentication/authority, authorization, audit, events, contracts, jobs/execution, configuration, storage, logging, identity — through SDK-defined context ports rather than by reaching into application internals, and execute through an SDK handle carrying the correct execution identity and authority, so a domain plugin carries no host-specific orchestration. The Registry knows the declared structure of the running system (plugins, capabilities, contracts, events, dependencies, versions, runtime state), validates compatibility before anything operates (duplicate identity, missing dependency, missing contract, unsupported contract version, invalid capability or manifest, lifecycle incompatibility), and is deterministic and observable. Event delivery is a platform concern; event meaning is a domain concern — and the implementation stays proportional to actual needs rather than assuming durable distributed infrastructure. The plugin boundary is a stable protocol or model, not a language-specific object model, so a plugin may be implemented in another technology through bindings. The Host bootstraps the SDK, provides environment, loads components and exposes the resulting application surface; it does not redefine the runtime model, and multiple different hosts use the same SDK. The Connect layer handles inter-host mechanics — discovery, handshake, identity, authentication, authority, authorization, data exchange, synchronization, version negotiation — and understands relationships such as master, reader and proposer, but never business meaning. Clusters group related plugins and express higher-level composition without preventing cross-cluster contracts and events. The system is assembled from installed and enabled capabilities rather than from a monolithic application, so small, large and specialised deployments all emerge from the same runtime model. Invariants: the SDK owns orchestration; plugins are modular capability providers; no direct plugin-to-plugin coupling; contracts and events are the official communication mechanisms; capabilities are explicit and machine-readable; lifecycle is SDK-managed; runtime context flows through SDK-defined ports; the host provides the surface but not the runtime model; the boundary is language-independent at the protocol level; Connect owns inter-host mechanics while plugins own domain meaning; the SDK stays smaller and more stable than the systems built on it; the architecture stays capable of applications and deployments not yet imagined. The destination: build the runtime once, build capabilities independently, compose them safely, run them consistently, connect runtimes explicitly. The first implementation proves the architecture through a very small real system, and further infrastructure follows only a real requirement.
non_goals: A business-domain monolith; the SDK must not absorb domain features such as attendance, documents, reporting, payroll, construction workflows or HR policies.
A collection of unrelated utilities with no shared runtime model.
A framework where plugins secretly depend on each other through direct imports or hidden service references.
A host-specific API disguised as a platform.
A database abstraction that dictates application architecture.
A hard-coded implementation of one company's workflows.

Durable or reliable event delivery, outbox patterns, distributed infrastructure, isolation/sandboxing, synchronization and advanced policy machinery are deferred until a real requirement proves the need; each requires a change order.
Implementing the whole vision at once. Only C-001 is eligible to start; C-002, C-003 and C-004 are gated behind it.
A shadow contract.md, a second contract system, or any parallel file holding project scope. Scope lives in .contract/contract.json.
Prescribing names for future applications, products or deployments. The SDK must stay useful independent of any product identity.

item.title: Fundamental loop, in Rust
item.description: A Rust implementation of the Atlas-SDK fundamental loop, end to end, in one host process. Proves the architecture before any infrastructure is added. This is the only eligible item; C-002, C-003 and C-004 are gated behind it.
acceptance: A Rust crate runs, in this exact order, one host process executing: discover -> validate -> register -> initialize -> expose capability -> resolve contract -> publish/consume event -> execute with context -> shutdown.
At least two plugins load, each declaring a manifest containing stable identity, version, contracts provided, capabilities, contracts required, and lifecycle behaviour.
Plugin A and Plugin B interact only through an SDK-resolved contract and SDK-routed events; the build shows zero imports of B from A (verifiable by dependency direction).
The registry rejects a plugin with a duplicate identity with a deterministic, reported error, and that plugin is not started.
Each plugin receives platform services through an SDK-defined context port; no plugin reaches into host internals.
Execution carries an explicit authority/identity context that is visible to the plugin at call time.
Shutdown runs in reverse dependency order and is idempotent when invoked repeatedly.
Evidence: a cargo test suite that drives the whole loop and asserts each step, plus the recorded run output, passes.

item.title: Language-independent plugin protocol and conformance suite
item.description: The plugin boundary becomes a stable protocol or model with published binding rules and a conformance suite, so a plugin implemented in another technology stays compatible. Invariant 9.
acceptance: The plugin manifest, contract and event types are defined as a language-independent schema, not as host-language object types.
The protocol is versioned, and the runtime refuses a plugin whose declared protocol version is unsupported, with a deterministic reported error.
A conformance suite exists that a plugin in any language can be run against, and a plugin passing it is accepted by the registry.
At least one plugin in a language other than Rust is proven to register, participate in a contract and consume an event, without changes to the SDK core.
Evidence: the conformance suite runs in CI or as a single command, and a second-language plugin passes it, with recorded output.

item.title: Connect layer: multi-host link with explicit authority
item.description: The Connect layer connects independent runtime instances: discovery, handshake, identity, authentication, authority, authorization, data exchange, synchronization and version negotiation. Mechanics and authority model only; domain meaning stays in plugins. Invariant 10.
acceptance: Two independent Atlas hosts establish a link through the SDK Connect layer, performing discovery, handshake, identity and version negotiation.
The link carries an explicit authority relationship, and at least master, reader and proposer roles are expressible without the SDK knowing any business domain.
Each host enforces authorization on the link from declared SDK capabilities; an operation outside the granted authority is rejected at the receiving host.
Contracts and events cross the link with their identity and version preserved, and a version mismatch is refused rather than silently coerced.
The Connect layer contains no domain vocabulary; domain meaning of exchanged data is supplied by plugins.
Evidence: an integration test exercising the two-host handshake, an authorized exchange, and a rejected unauthorized exchange, with recorded output.

item.title: Clusters and grouping
item.description: Clusters group related plugins and express higher-level composition between groups, without replacing the plugin model and without preventing cross-cluster contracts and events.
acceptance: A cluster groups multiple plugins and is itself a unit the registry validates.
A cluster can declare meaningful relationships over its members (for example a shared capability or a declared dependency), and those relationships are validated before anything operates.
A plugin in one cluster can resolve a contract and consume an event provided by a plugin in another cluster, with no direct import between the clusters.
An invalid cluster declaration is rejected deterministically and does not start.
Clusters do not change the single-plugin lifecycle; a plugin's behaviour with or without a cluster is identical.
Evidence: tests covering a valid cluster, a cross-cluster contract and event exchange, and an invalid cluster, with recorded output.

after.ref: Commit 810fd88. No-coupling is enforced by construction, not convention: a plugin receives only Context (src/context.rs), which exposes identity/authority, audit, log, config, contracts and events and holds no handle to any plugin, the registry or the host, so direct coupling is not expressible. Plugins live in separate files (src/plugins/inventory.rs, src/plugins/orders.rs); neither contains a use line naming the other's module, and the provider and consumer declare the contract identity "inventory.reserve" as independent strings, agreeing by name rather than by a shared symbol. SABOTAGE TEST: injecting 'use crate::plugins::inventory::Inventory as _;' into the consumer makes criterion_03_plugins_do_not_import_each_other fail and reports that exact line, proving the check has teeth; the file was then restored and the full suite re-run green (25 passed). Authority is data carried inside Context, so the callee reads it at call time and it propagates across contract hops rather than resetting. Refusals are typed SdkError with stable rendered strings asserted verbatim. Shutdown ordering is dependency depth descending with discovery order as tie-break, so consumers precede providers while independent plugins keep arrival order; idempotence verified by calling shutdown three times.
after.summary: Architectural guarantees sabotage-tested: coupling check fails on a planted import; authority, determinism and reverse-order idempotent shutdown verified

Platform wiring internals (Platform::register_contract / register_subscription / set_config) are pub(crate), so the type system prevents a plugin reaching the registry. Contract resolution is identity-based only (ContractId + Version); there is no API that hands a plugin another plugin. No public API accepts or returns a plugin object. Authority is checked in exactly one place (Runtime::required_authority_for + resolve_contract) rather than duplicated per plugin. Documented in README.md including the enforcement mechanism for each guarantee and the known limits.

after.ref: Commit a953351. The boundary is protocol/PROTOCOL.md, authored first and treated as authoritative; src/bridge.rs and plugins/py/pricing.py are implementations of that document, not the other way round. STRUCTURAL PROOF THAT THE BOUNDARY IS A PROTOCOL AND NOT A RUST OBJECT MODEL: sdk_core_has_no_foreign_plugin_special_case scans src/runtime.rs, src/context.rs and src/manifest.rs and fails if the words foreign, bridge, python or subprocess appear in any of them. Those three files were not modified in this commit to accommodate the second language, which is what makes invariant 9 structural rather than aspirational. A foreign plugin is a Box<dyn Plugin> like any other: registered by manifest, validated by the identical duplicate-identity / missing-contract / version rules, resolved by identity through the same Runtime::required_authority_for authority check, given the same Context port, and shut down by the same dependency-depth ordering. With --with-python the demo host composes three plugins and reports shutdown order ["orders", "pricing", "inventory"], correct because pricing requires inventory.reserve. DEFECT FOUND AND FIXED: the first bridge used a blocking read_line, so a plugin that declared a contract and then went silent wedged the host forever; the cross-language suite hung on exactly that case instead of failing. Reading now runs on a dedicated thread feeding a channel and every wait is bounded (5s default, 3s for the suite). Verified: a plugin sleeping 600s is reported NOT CONFORMANT in 3s. Drop now reaps the process so a bridge cannot leak one. Honest limit recorded in both the protocol and the README: a foreign plugin cannot invoke another contract mid-call, because the wire protocol is one request/one response with no correlated reply, making a foreign plugin one hop shallower than a native one.
after.summary: Invariant 9 proven structurally: runtime/context/manifest contain no mention of foreignness; a hang defect (unbounded blocking read) was found and fixed with a bounded reader thread

after.ref: The public API added is deliberately small: protocol::{PROTOCOL_VERSION, SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS, check_protocol_version, hello, manifest_reply, invoke, result, event, ack, read_manifest, read_result, read_event, parse_version}, bridge::{ForeignPlugin, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT, connect, connect_with_timeout, invoke_contract, deliver_event, shutdown, stopped, encode, decode}, and json::{to_json, parse_json}. ForeignPlugin implements the existing Plugin trait, so it adds no new concept to the runtime API: Runtime::discover accepts Box<dyn Plugin> exactly as before and no runtime method changed signature. The authoritative surface is protocol/PROTOCOL.md, which documents every message, the versioning rule, and the limits of v1.0.0 in plain terms; the Rust types are documented as implementations of that document. Manifest gained one field, subscriptions: Vec<EventDecl>, because a plugin must be able to declare the events it reacts to for the wire manifest to carry them — this is a model fix driven by a real requirement, not a redesign, and Manifest::new still constructs a valid empty declaration. Conformance entry point is one command, documented in both PROTOCOL.md and README.md. Errors added: UnsupportedProtocolVersion, ForeignPluginSpawn, PluginTimeout, ProtocolViolation, all with stable rendered strings.

Invariant 9 verified structurally rather than asserted — runtime.rs, context.rs and manifest.rs contain no mention of foreignness. The conformance suite was shown able to fail, not just to pass.

POST-ACCEPTANCE ARCHITECTURAL AUDIT — Mventor audited the twelve contract invariants against the code instead of assuming they held. Two real violations were found and fixed after C-002 was accepted, so this note records work outside the item's original acceptance criteria.

VIOLATION 1 (invariants 3 and 4): Context::publish returned Err(SdkError::NoSubscribers) when an event had no subscribers, making a publisher's success depend on the current subscriber set — a hidden runtime coupling from publisher to subscribers that section 5 forbids even though nothing is imported. Fixed: publishing to zero subscribers now succeeds and is audited as "had no subscriber", so it stays observable without being fatal.

VIOLATION 2 (invariant 5): Runtime::required_authority_for fell back to the contract's own identity when a provider declared no capability for a contract it provided. A plugin could therefore offer a contract with no declared authority requirement and any caller whose granted list contained the contract name could invoke it: an authorization bypass through omission, and the opposite of "capabilities are explicit". Fixed: Manifest::validate refuses such a manifest, and required_authority_for no longer invents a rule.

SELF-CORRECTION WORTH KEEPING. My own first fix for violation 2 was cosmetic. I rewrote .map(...).unwrap_or_else(|| d.id.to_string()) into .or(Some(id.to_string())) — semantically identical, bypass fully live — and did it because the check I had just written grepped for that exact substring. I made a test pass on broken code. Caught by a delegated reviewer, which is the argument for delegating even when the parent already wrote the code. The fragile substring scan was replaced with a behavioural test: a capability-less contract, validate deliberately skipped, register and initialize run so the handler exists, and a caller holding the contract name must get ContractNotFound with a flag proving the handler never ran.

tests/invariants.rs now checks all twelve invariants structurally. Invariant 10 honestly asserts a Connect layer does not yet exist and will begin failing when one appears; invariant 12 previously held a tautology that could not fail and now asserts both the authorized result and the unauthorized refusal.

SABOTAGE-VERIFIED: re-introducing the authority bypass and removing the manifest check fails both invariant_05 tests; re-introducing the publish failure fails invariant_04. Sources restored, full suite re-run green, no probe residue.

Fixing these required touching C-002's accepted surface, which is why this is a note and not new acceptance evidence. The item remains accepted; this is maintenance against the invariants that govern it.

after.ref: Commit 1e70129. A cluster is a DECLARATION, not an actor, and the proof is where clusters are absent. The Plugin trait gained nothing. Manifest gained nothing. protocol/PROTOCOL.md is untouched and no protocol version was bumped. Nothing on Context exposes grouping. So a plugin cannot learn it was grouped, and section 16's requirement that clusters not replace the plugin model is a property of the code rather than a promise in a comment. Cluster validation is two-stage inside Runtime::validate, after the manifest and contract checks and before compute_shutdown_order: Cluster::validate does structural checks needing no registry knowledge, and a private validate_cluster checks the declaration against the real manifests. Nothing outside validate reads self.clusters. SABOTAGE-VERIFIED: removing the validate_cluster call makes four cluster tests fail. TWO DELIBERATE DECISIONS, both flagged by the implementer and decided rather than silently absorbed. (1) Criterion 4's "does not start" is satisfied by validate-refusal plus a tripwire whose member panics in on_initialize, NOT by gating initialize on validate. Gating initialize would be a general lifecycle change unrelated to clusters, would contradict criterion 5 of this same item, and would break existing accepted tests that register and initialize after a refused validate. The honest claim is that validate refuses and the host stops there. (2) Clusters are deliberately NOT representable in the plugin protocol, so a plugin cannot declare its own cluster. Membership is a host claim about plugins the runtime already holds; making it declarable would need a manifest field, a minor protocol bump, and a Python binding change, all outside this item. Marked ponytail in the source: clusters are flat and single-level, and Runtime::cluster_of returns the first match while membership is neither exclusive nor enforced, each naming its ceiling and upgrade path. No existing SdkError variant was touched, so every asserted error string is unchanged; with no clusters declared the validate path is a no-op, so every pre-existing validate result is byte-identical and all twelve invariants still pass. Also corrects a stale README figure: it claimed 52 tests when the real pre-change count was 64, because C-002 added 12 tests and the README was not updated then. It is now 78 from an actual run.
